title: From Cayley-Hamilton to Compact Operators: The Infinite-Dimensional Bridge
content: The header frames the central question: the parent OQ-01 showed efficient Cayley-Hamilton reduction for sparse matrices. In infinite dimensions, there is no finite-degree characteristic polynomial. The file identifies compact operators as the natural setting for the analog, and outlines the three-part answer: discrete spectrum (Riesz-Schauder), Fredholm alternative, and spectral projection decomposition. The formalization uses Mathlib's ContinuousLinearMap, InnerProductSpace, and IsCompact.
mathContext: In finite dimensions, $A \in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ satisfies its characteristic polynomial: $\text{charpoly}(A)(A) = 0$. This fails in infinite dimensions: a bounded operator $T: H \to H$ on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space has no finite-degree characteristic polynomial. The remedy: restrict to **compact operators** (those mapping bounded sets to relatively compact sets), which inherit a 'discrete' spectral theory analogous to the finite-dimensional case.

title: Compact Operators: The 'Good' Infinite-Dimensional Operators
content: IsCompactOp T is defined as IsCompact (closure (T '' Metric.closedBall 0 1)). This is the standard definition: T maps the closed unit ball to a relatively compact set. Proved: compactOp_zero (zero maps everything to the compact set {0}), compactOp_smul (scalar multiples preserve compactness via continuous image), compactOp_comp_left (bounded composed with compact is compact, since continuous images of compact sets are compact). Three sorries: compactOp_sum and compactOp_comp_right require Minkowski sum and generalized ball arguments.
mathContext: $T \in \mathcal{B}(H)$ is **compact** if $\overline{T(B_1)}$ is compact, where $B_1 = \{x : \|x\| \leq 1\}$. Equivalently: $T$ is the norm-limit of finite-rank operators. The compact operators $\mathcal{K}(H)$ form a closed two-sided ideal in $\mathcal{B}(H)$: $\mathcal{K}(H)$ is closed under $+$, $\cdot$, and $S \circ T$ and $T \circ S$ for $S \in \mathcal{B}(H)$, $T \in \mathcal{K}(H)$.

title: Discrete Spectrum: The Infinite-Dimensional Characteristic Polynomial
content: Defines IsEigenvalue and Eigenspace. Proves eigenspace_is_subspace: eigenspaces are closed under 0, addition, and scalar multiplication (using map_zero, map_add, map_smul, smul_comm). compact_spectrum_discrete (axiom): the eigenvalues of a compact operator form a sequence converging to 0. finite_multiplicity: each nonzero eigenvalue has finite-dimensional eigenspace (stated via a cardinality bound on orthogonal sets). The discrete spectrum replaces the roots of the characteristic polynomial.
mathContext: For compact $T \in \mathcal{K}(H)$: $\sigma(T) \setminus \{0\}$ is at most countable, each point is an eigenvalue with finite multiplicity, and $0$ is the only possible accumulation point. This is the **Riesz-Schauder theorem**. Compare: in $M_n$, $\text{charpoly}(A)$ has at most $n$ roots; for compact $T$, the 'roots' (eigenvalues) converge to $0$. The eigenspace $\ker(\lambda I - T)$ is finite-dimensional for $\lambda \neq 0$, analogous to multiplicity $\leq n$.

title: The Fredholm Alternative: Precisely Analogous to Cayley-Hamilton
content: fredholm_alternative (axiom): for compact T and nonzero lambda, either (lambda I - T) is bijective or lambda is an eigenvalue. No continuous spectrum. no_continuous_spectrum_at_nonzero is proved by case analysis on the Fredholm alternative using absurd. This is the precise analog: Cayley-Hamilton says the eigenvalues are exactly the spectral obstructions; the Fredholm alternative says the same for compact operators, with the additional guarantee of no continuous spectrum.
mathContext: **Fredholm alternative** (1903): For compact $T$ and $\lambda \neq 0$: $\lambda I - T$ is bijective $\iff$ $\ker(\lambda I - T) = 0$ $\iff$ $\lambda \notin \sigma_p(T)$. **No continuous spectrum**: for compact $T$, $\sigma(T) \setminus \{0\} = \sigma_p(T) \setminus \{0\}$ (point spectrum only). In finite dimensions, this is trivially true by rank-nullity. In infinite dimensions, it requires compactness of $T$ and fails for general bounded operators.

title: The Three-Pillar Analogy: Cayley-Hamilton vs Compact Operator Spectral Theory
content: cayley_hamilton_analogy packages the three analogs: (1) Fredholm alternative at every nonzero lambda, (2) discrete spectrum with eigenvalues converging to 0, (3) spectral projections at each eigenvalue. Proved by combining fredholm_alternative, compact_spectrum_discrete, and spectral_decomposition_exists. The summary table maps: charpoly -> spectral structure, roots -> eigenvalues, degree n -> eigenvalues -> 0, polynomial reduction -> spectral projection decomposition.
mathContext:
| **Finite dim** | **Compact operator** |
|---|---|
| $\text{charpoly}(A)$ degree $n$ | $\sigma(T)$ at most countable, $\lambda_k \to 0$ |
| $\text{charpoly}(A)(A) = 0$ | Fredholm: $\lambda I - T$ bijective or eigenvalue |
| $f(A) \equiv f \mod \text{charpoly}$ | $f(T) P_\lambda$ depends on $f$ near $\lambda$ |

Compact operators bridge the gap because $\mathcal{K}(H) = \overline{\mathcal{F}(H)}$ (norm-closure of finite-rank operators).
